blocks.text: A slider moves outward along the arm of a rotating packaging sorter at 1.5 m/s while the arm turns at 4 rad/s. Even though the slider's speed along the arm is constant, it is accelerating sideways at 12 m/s$^2$, and the arm must push it with a real force. That extra sideways term is the Coriolis acceleration.

blocks.markdown: When a point $P$ moves along or within a rotating body, the simplest way to describe the motion is relative to a frame fixed in that body. The frame turns with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega$ (rad/s) and angular acceleration $\boldsymbol\alpha$ (rad/s$^2$). Differentiating the position twice, and accounting for the turning of the frame's unit vectors, gives the acceleration of $P$ measured in the fixed (absolute) frame.

blocks.caption: $\mathbf r$ is the position of $P$ from the frame origin O, $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ and $\mathbf a_{\text{rel}}$ are the velocity and acceleration of $P$ measured in the rotating frame, and $\mathbf a_O$ is the absolute acceleration of the origin (zero if O is fixed).

blocks.title: The four terms (origin fixed)
blocks.text: With O fixed, $\mathbf a_O=0$ and four terms remain: (1) the **relative acceleration** $\mathbf a_{\text{rel}}$, (2) the **Coriolis acceleration** $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$, (3) the **tangential (Euler) acceleration** $\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r$ and (4) the **centripetal acceleration** $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)=-\omega^2\mathbf r$. If the origin moves, add $\mathbf a_O$ as a fifth term.

blocks.markdown: For a collar on a straight radial rod in the plane, use polar components with $\hat e_r$ along the rod and $\hat e_\theta$ turned $90^\circ$ in the direction of positive (counterclockwise) rotation. The Coriolis term $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ has magnitude $2\omega\dot r$ and points along $\hat e_\theta$ when both $\omega$ and $\dot r$ are positive.

blocks.caption: Radial and transverse components of acceleration of a collar at distance $r$ from the pivot; $\dot r$ and $\ddot r$ are the collar's velocity and acceleration along the rod.

blocks.title: Coriolis acceleration of a collar
blocks.prompt: A collar slides outward along a rod at a constant 1.5 m/s relative to the rod, while the rod turns counterclockwise at a constant 4 rad/s. Find the Coriolis acceleration and its direction.

steps.text: Direction: $\boldsymbol\omega=+4\hat k$ and $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=1.5\hat e_r$, and $\hat k\times\hat e_r=\hat e_\theta$.

blocks.answer: $a_C=12$ m/s$^2$ perpendicular to the rod, in the sense of rotation (counterclockwise).

blocks.title: All terms for a collar
blocks.prompt: At the instant considered the collar is 0.6 m from O, moving outward on the rod at 1.5 m/s with $\ddot r=2.0$ m/s$^2$. The rod has $\omega=4$ rad/s and $\alpha=3$ rad/s$^2$, both counterclockwise. Find the absolute acceleration components.

steps.text: Radial component: relative acceleration plus centripetal term.
Transverse component: Euler term plus Coriolis term.

blocks.answer: $a_r=-7.6$ m/s$^2$ (toward O), $a_\theta=13.8$ m/s$^2$ and $|a|=15.75$ m/s$^2$. The Coriolis term is the largest single contribution.

blocks.caption: Terms in the acceleration of a collar on a rotating rod.

blocks.markdown: **Direction rule.** $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ is perpendicular to both vectors. In the plane, the Coriolis acceleration is $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ rotated $90^\circ$ in the **sense of $\boldsymbol\omega$**. If the collar moves outward and the rod turns counterclockwise, it points counterclockwise-tangentially. If the collar moves inward, or if $\omega$ reverses, its direction reverses. It vanishes if either $\omega=0$ or $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol\omega$.

blocks.title: Why it exists
blocks.text: The collar's radial velocity changes direction as the rod turns, and the collar's transverse velocity ($r\omega$) changes magnitude as it moves outward. Each effect contributes $\omega\dot r$, giving a total of $2\omega\dot r$. It is not a force; it appears because the observer is rotating.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Omitting the factor 2, forgetting the sign of $\dot r$ for an inward-moving collar, and mixing up the Coriolis term with the Euler term $r\alpha$, which depends on $\alpha$ and not on $\dot r$.

items: Collar fixed on the rod ($\dot r=\ddot r=0$): only $-r\omega^2$ and $r\alpha$ remain.
Constant $\omega$ and constant $\dot r$: only $-r\omega^2$ (radial) and $2\dot r\omega$ (transverse).
Add $\mathbf a_O$ if the frame origin itself accelerates.

points: The absolute acceleration of a point in a rotating frame is the sum of relative, Coriolis, tangential and centripetal terms (plus $\mathbf a_O$ if the origin accelerates).
For a collar on a radial rod: $a_r=\ddot r-r\omega^2$ and $a_\theta=r\alpha+2\dot r\omega$.
Coriolis acceleration $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ is perpendicular to the rod, turned in the sense of $\boldsymbol\omega$ for outward motion.

questions.stem: A rod rotates counterclockwise about O and a collar slides outward along it. In which direction does the Coriolis acceleration of the collar act?

options.text: Perpendicular to the rod, in the clockwise sense
Perpendicular to the rod, in the counterclockwise sense

questions.correctOptionText: Perpendicular to the rod, in the counterclockwise sense

distractorRationale.a: The Coriolis term is a cross product, so it is perpendicular to the relative velocity.
distractorRationale.b: That is the direction of the centripetal term $-r\omega^2$.
distractorRationale.c: This is the direction when the collar moves inward or the rotation is clockwise.

questions.explanation: $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ with $\boldsymbol\omega=+\hat k$ and $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ along $+\hat e_r$ gives $+\hat e_\theta$, the counterclockwise transverse direction. Reversing either vector reverses the Coriolis acceleration.

questions.stem: A collar slides inward along a rotating rod at 0.8 m/s relative to the rod, while the rod turns at a constant 6 rad/s. Find the magnitude of the Coriolis acceleration in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: The magnitude is $2\omega|\dot r|=2(6)(0.8)=9.6$ m/s$^2$. Because the collar moves inward the direction is opposite to that for outward motion, but the magnitude is the same.

questions.stem: A point $P$ moves in a frame that rotates about a fixed origin O with variable angular velocity. Which list gives the four terms of its absolute acceleration?

options.text: Relative, Coriolis, tangential ($\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r$) and centripetal ($\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)$)

questions.correctOptionText: Relative, Coriolis, tangential ($\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r$) and centripetal ($\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)$)

distractorRationale.b: Gravity is a force, not a term in the kinematic transport relation.
distractorRationale.c: Drag is not a kinematic term.
distractorRationale.d: With a fixed origin $\mathbf a_O=0$ and the relative acceleration $\mathbf a_{\text{rel}}$ is a term.

questions.explanation: The transport relation with $\mathbf a_O=0$ is $\mathbf a=\mathbf a_{\text{rel}}+2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}+\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)$. Each corresponds to a distinct physical effect.

questions.stem: A collar is 0.40 m from the pivot of a rod turning at a constant 2.5 rad/s counterclockwise. It slides outward at a constant 1.2 m/s relative to the rod. Find the magnitude in m/s$^2$ of its absolute acceleration.
questions.explanation: With $\ddot r=0$ and $\alpha=0$: $a_r=-r\omega^2=-0.4(6.25)=-2.5$ m/s$^2$ and $a_\theta=2\dot r\omega=2(1.2)(2.5)=6.0$ m/s$^2$. The magnitude is $\sqrt{2.5^2+6.0^2}=6.5$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem: Take counterclockwise as positive and $\hat e_\theta$ as the counterclockwise transverse direction. A collar is 0.50 m from O on a rod with $\omega=3$ rad/s and $\alpha=-2$ rad/s$^2$. The collar moves inward at $\dot r=-1.0$ m/s with $\ddot r=0.8$ m/s$^2$. Find the transverse component $a_\theta$ of the absolute acceleration in m/s$^2$ (signed).
questions.explanation: The transverse component is $a_\theta=r\alpha+2\dot r\omega=0.5(-2)+2(-1.0)(3)=-1.0-6.0=-7.0$ m/s$^2$. Both terms are negative here, so the transverse acceleration is clockwise.

questions.stem: A rod turns clockwise about O and a collar moves outward along it. Compared with the same motion on a counterclockwise-turning rod, the Coriolis acceleration of the collar is

options.text: equal in magnitude and the same direction
equal in magnitude but opposite in direction

questions.correctOptionText: equal in magnitude but opposite in direction

distractorRationale.a: Coriolis acceleration vanishes only if $\omega=0$ or $v_{\text{rel}}$ is parallel to $\omega$.
distractorRationale.d: The magnitude $2\omega v_{\text{rel}}$ depends only on $|\omega|$.

questions.explanation: $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ changes sign when $\boldsymbol\omega$ reverses with $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ unchanged. The magnitude remains $2|\omega|v_{\text{rel}}$.

questions.stem: A fluid particle moves outward along a straight radial passage in a rotor that spins at a constant 30 rev/min. Its speed relative to the passage is 12 m/s. Find the magnitude of its Coriolis acceleration in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: The angular speed is $\omega=30(2\pi)/60=3.1416$ rad/s. The Coriolis acceleration is $2\omega v_{\text{rel}}=2(3.1416)(12)=75.4$ m/s$^2$, which is about 7.7 times $g$.

questions.stem: A collar is clamped at a fixed distance $r$ on a rod turning with constant angular velocity $\omega$. Which terms of its absolute acceleration are non-zero?

options.text: Only the centripetal term, of magnitude $r\omega^2$ toward O

questions.correctOptionText: Only the centripetal term, of magnitude $r\omega^2$ toward O

distractorRationale.b: With no relative velocity the Coriolis term is zero.
distractorRationale.d: The tangential term needs $\alpha\ne0$, and $\alpha=0$ here.

questions.explanation: With $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=0$, $\mathbf a_{\text{rel}}=0$ and $\boldsymbol\alpha=0$, only $\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r)=-\omega^2\mathbf r$ remains. This is ordinary circular motion.

questions.stem: Explain physically why a body sliding radially along a rotating rod has a transverse (Coriolis) acceleration, and state its magnitude and the rule for its direction. Say when it is zero.
markingGuide: Moving outward changes the transverse velocity $r\omega$ at rate $\dot r\omega$
Turning of the rod rotates the radial velocity vector at rate $\omega\dot r$, a second equal contribution
Direction: $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ rotated $90^\circ$ in the sense of $\boldsymbol\omega$ (from $2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$)
Zero when $\omega=0$ or $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=0$ (or parallel to $\boldsymbol\omega$)
questions.explanation: The two equal contributions explain the factor 2. The direction follows the right-hand rule on the cross product, and reverses if the slide direction or the rotation sense reverses.

questions.stem: A slider moves along an arm that rotates about a pivot O, and the pivot itself is on a carriage with acceleration $\mathbf a_O$. Write the expression for the slider's absolute acceleration, identify every term and say which terms vanish if the slider is locked to the arm and the arm turns at constant speed.
markingGuide: Identifies the origin term, relative term, Coriolis term, tangential term and centripetal term
Defines $\mathbf r$, $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ and $\boldsymbol\omega$ with the frame
Locked slider: $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=\mathbf a_{\text{rel}}=0$ so relative and Coriolis terms vanish
Constant speed: $\boldsymbol\alpha=0$ so the tangential term vanishes, leaving $\mathbf a_O$ plus centripetal
questions.explanation: The five-term form reduces to the four-term form when the origin is fixed. Setting the relative motion and $\alpha$ to zero leaves rigid-body motion: translation of O plus centripetal acceleration.
